claims.text: Pulumi's component state migrations let component authors ship an upgrade path with the component itself; a migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change.
Pulumi component state migrations are new.
The Pulumi component state migrations API is experimental and may change.

The v1 example uses the legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component, creating a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway, with a security group outside the component referring to the VPC.
Replacing a VPC would require replacing the security group too, because the security group refers to the VPC's ID (per AWS CloudFormation EC2 SecurityGroup VpcId docs).
Without a migration connecting old state to new code, a Pulumi upgrade could replace the VPC instead of keeping it.
The example does not create a database.
A replacement database does not automatically contain the old database's data.
The second version of the example upgrades to the modern `awsx.ec2.Vpc` component while keeping the existing network.
The third version of the example removes AWSX and declares resources directly with `@pulumi/aws`.
Across all three example versions, the AWS resource IDs stay the same and the security group continues to use the same VPC.

The Pulumi resource trees for v1, v2 and v3 of the example are structured as shown (legacy awsx:x:ec2 components with subnet and internet gateway wrappers; modern awsx:ec2:Vpc without wrappers; plain aws resources in v3).
Pulumi state records both physical resources and components; each record has a Pulumi name called a URN, and managed resources also have a cloud provider ID.
The legacy AWSX component wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components, while modern AWSX removes those wrappers and puts managed resources under different parents.
In the example, the Pulumi name of the subnet changes from `vpc-isolated-0` to `vpc-isolated-1`.
Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible, but cannot remove component wrappers and transfer references.
Pulumi resource options accept a `stateMigrations` option taking migration callbacks, and the new VPC component is registered with an alias for the legacy component type.
The example's migration file exists at aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts in pulumi/examples and exports `migrateClassicVpc`.
The alias lets Pulumi find the old component, and the migration callback receives its saved state followed by the state of its children.

The migration callback returns `newState` (the complete set of records replacing the old component and its children) and `successors` (a map from each disappearing old URN to the URN that replaces it).
The example callback is safe to run again, doing nothing if state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources, and raises an error on an unexpected component type.
The example's `rename` helper copies the saved record and changes its URN, type, and parent while preserving the AWS resource ID and other saved fields.
Pulumi uses `successors` mappings to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack, keeping the security group's reference to the VPC valid after migration.

The third example version declares the VPC, subnet, route table, association, and internet gateway directly with `@pulumi/aws`; the second migration removes the AWSX VPC component record and maps both the old component and its VPC child to the new VPC record, keeping the AWS ID.
The VPC registration in the v3 example keeps aliases for both previous component types and both migration callbacks.

Pulumi runs state migration callbacks in order, passing each result to the next; a stack on legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to plain AWS, a stack on modern AWSX skips the first migration, and after both run the callbacks return no result on later updates.

After a migration changes saved state, Pulumi compares the new program with that state and calls the provider for remaining changes; the example can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags.
Running `pulumi preview` evaluates the migration without saving it, and `pulumi up` saves the migrated state.
Before each upgrade in the example, the preview should show no creates, deletes, or replacements for the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group.
When a component registers its migration in its implementation, users do not need to write the migration or edit stack state, and Pulumi runs it as part of normal preview and update.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ covering the callback contract.
A GitHub discussion exists at pulumi/pulumi discussions/24799 for component state migrations feedback.
The VPC example in pulumi/examples contains all three programs and the migration code.
State migration callbacks (the Pulumi resource option) run during previews and updates when prior state exists.
State migration callbacks must be idempotent and return no result when the state no longer needs migration.
State migration callbacks rewrite state without performing provider operations.
A Pulumi component state migration is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A Pulumi component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings.
In a component state migration result, each successor mapping connects an old URN omitted from the result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, a component state migration callback returns no result.
The state entries in a component state migration callback use the checkpoint resource format, including fields such as urn, type, id, parent, provider, inputs, and outputs.
The option reference page at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/statemigrations/#callback-api explains the callback API.
A component state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using update plans or targeted updates.
The restrictions on state-changing migration results (for update plans or targeted updates) do not require removing an already-applied migration.
